title: Output of the `project.list` MCP tool
description:
The whole response. `project.list` is the tool an agent calls to find out what this daemon can answer for, so its shape is as much of the contract as a search result's is — and it went unpublished for three milestones while the tools around it were described in detail.

Four keys, always all four. `projects` is what can be queried, `unreadable` is what the registry holds and nothing can serve, `count` sizes the first of those, and `remedy` says what to do about the second. `projects` and `unreadable` are two independent reads of the same file, not a partition of one snapshot: `load()` keeps the entries whose key builds as a `ProjectId` *and* whose value names a root path, `unreadable_ids()` reports the ids that fail either test, and a registration landing between the two reads can leave an id in both lists or in neither. Do not compute the size of the registry by adding `count` and the length of `unreadable`, and do not treat membership in one as proof of absence from the other.

count.description: The number of entries in `projects`, and nothing else. It answers "how many projects can I query", so it excludes the unreadable ids — an entry naming no root path can be queried by nothing. It is not the size of the registry file: `projects` and `unreadable` are independent reads of that file, not a partition, so their lengths do not sum to a count of anything.

projects.description: Every registration this daemon could read, sorted by id. Deliberately narrower than `theurian project list`, which prints each entry whole: only the two fields a caller acts on cross the wire.

projectId.description:
The id to pass as `projectId` to every project-scoped tool (ADR-0002).

**Constrained, and it was not always.** This value is a *key* of the registry file, which lives in the user's home directory and is hand-edited. While keys went unvalidated, `load()` published whatever the file held: a key of `""` or `"Team One/API"` with a valid `rootPath` was published here verbatim, and then refused by every project-scoped tool and by `theurian project unregister` — the escape command's remedy pointing back at the command that printed the id. A pattern would have rejected the product's own output, so this field carried none, and said that the pattern would belong here once key validation reached the file read.

It has. `_usable_id` now excludes from `load()` any key that cannot be constructed as a `ProjectId`, and reports it through `unreadable` instead. So the promise `projects` makes is once again true — an id published here is an id every project-scoped surface accepts — and the constraint above is what holds the schema to it. The bounds mirror `ProjectId._validate` exactly: 1 to 200 characters, lowercase kebab-case.

**The trailing `\n?` this pattern carried until Milestone 5 was load-bearing, and what changed is the constructor rather than the reasoning.** `ProjectId` validated against a `$`-anchored Python `re`, whose `$` matches at end of input *or immediately before a trailing newline*, so `ProjectId("demo\n")` constructed. A registry hand-edited to `{"demo\n": {"rootPath": "/valid"}}` was therefore loaded and published here — reproduced by calling the tool against exactly that file, which answered with `"demo"` and `"demo\n"` in one array, two entries a reader sees as one id. A bare slug pattern would have rejected that real response in exactly the ECMA-262 and RE2 clients this schema is published for, so the concession was what kept the schema true of its own product. The fix that anchored every pattern in `domain/identifiers.py` with `\A`/`\Z` removed the input, not the argument: `ProjectId("demo\n")` no longer constructs, and nothing can publish the value the `\n?` existed to admit.

**Which leaves it pointing the wrong way, and that much is simply false now.** Under ECMA-262 and RE2 a `\n?` tail admits a value the constructor refuses — the defect it was written to prevent, with the sign flipped. Measured under `node` and Go against `ProjectId` itself: the form above agrees with the constructor exactly in both dialects, and is loose by one string per accepted id — the id with a single trailing newline — under a Python-backed validator, where the `\n?` form was loose by two. Exactness in all three is not on offer. The form that has it ends `(?![\s\S])`, and RE2 will not compile a negative lookahead at all (`invalid or unsupported Perl syntax: (?!`), which is a worse failure than admitting a shape nothing emits. Over-acceptance under-documents; under-acceptance breaks the product — and it is now the bare `$` that over-accepts.

**No Python-backed test can see the difference, which is now the hazard rather than the alibi.** `jsonschema` evaluates `pattern` through Python's `re`, so `demo\n` satisfies this field under either form and the suite stays green while the schema and the domain drift apart. That is why the `\n?` could not be defended by a failing test when it was added, and why its removal cannot be defended by one either. Both directions were settled by running the patterns under `node` and Go rather than under the suite, which is the treatment the next `$` written into a published schema will need.

rootPath.description: Absolute path to the repository the id resolves to. Never empty: an entry naming no root, or naming `""` — which resolves to whatever directory the reading process happens to be in — is precisely what makes an entry unreadable, and such an entry appears in `unreadable` instead of here.

unreadable.description:
Ids present in the registry that `load()` skips, sorted. An entry is skipped for either of two reasons: its value names no root path, or its key cannot be constructed as a `ProjectId`.

Published because a skipped entry that nothing reports is a project that disappeared in silence, and because the id is the argument `theurian project unregister` needs — a remedy naming an id no surface prints is not a remedy. Every other tool refuses these ids; this is where a caller finds out why.

**Always present, empty array included.** Emitting the key only when it is non-empty makes "nothing is unreadable" indistinguishable from "this daemon predates the field", and a client that has to branch on key presence eventually forgets to.

**Unconstrained strings, and the pattern on `projectId` above is precisely why.** These are the keys that failed that pattern, plus the entries that named no root; applying it here would forbid the values this array exists to report, and a validator would reject the one response a user needs in order to repair the file. An unreadable id is whatever a hand edit left behind — spaces, quotes, an empty string — and it is carried verbatim so it can be copied into the command that removes it.

remedy.description:
What to do about `unreadable`, or `null` when it is empty.

Null-carrying rather than absent, which is the convention `retrieval-metadata.schema.json` already holds: one shape on every response, so a client never branches on key presence. `theurian project list` emits its equivalent key only when it applies; that is a rendering choice for a human reading one command's output, and it is not what a wire contract should ask a client to handle.

Generic rather than naming the ids. `unreadable` is where the ids are, and a remedy that repeated them would be a second copy free to drift from the list beside it.
